abstract: Objective: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) is a non-invasive neuromodulation technique with potential effects on pain perception. However, tSCS itself can evoke discomfort or pain at higher current intensities, and it remains unclear whether high-frequency tSCS alters the pain evoked by subsequent low-frequency stimulation. This study examined whether high-frequency cervical tSCS delivered at motor-threshold intensity is followed by changes in pain ratings elicited by low-frequency tSCS in healthy participants. Approach: Twenty-five healthy participants completed a single experimental session. Individual sensory, motor, and pain thresholds were determined using single-pulse tSCS at the C6-C7 spinal level. Pain was assessed using 1-Hz stimulation delivered for 1 min at an individually defined intensity corresponding to 6-7 points on a 0-10 Numerical Rating Scale. Participants then received 80-Hz tSCS for 10 min at motor-threshold intensity, followed by three repeated pain-assessment sessions separated by 5-min intervals. Surface electromyography was recorded from the flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis. Pain analysis included 25 participants, whereas EMG analysis included 18 participants. Main results: Pain ratings were significantly lower than baseline during the second and third post-stimulation assessments. In contrast, ratings obtained immediately after high-frequency stimulation did not differ significantly from baseline. EMG responses showed substantial inter-participant variability. No EMG metric showed a significant omnibus session effect after correction for multiple comparisons, although exploratory comparisons indicated transient increases in ECR AUC and mean rectified amplitude immediately after high-frequency stimulation. Significance: These findings indicate that high-frequency cervical tSCS can exert a measurable short-term influence on pain perception. Pain ratings and stimulation-evoked EMG responses showed different temporal patterns and represent complementary, non-equivalent outcomes of spinal stimulation.
